name: Gauss's Law
statement: The electric flux out of any closed surface equals the charge trapped inside it, divided by a constant.
statementAccent: equals the charge trapped inside it
meaning: Gauss's law states that the total electric flux passing outward through any closed surface is proportional to the total electric charge enclosed within it, equal to that charge divided by the permittivity of free space. In differential form, the divergence of the electric field at a point equals the charge density there divided by the same constant. It is one of Maxwell's four equations, the foundations of electromagnetism, and it captures the fact that electric field lines begin and end on charges. Only the charge inside the surface contributes to the net flux; external charges push field lines in one side and out the other, contributing nothing net. Gauss's law is both a deep statement about how charge sources the electric field and a powerful shortcut for computing fields in symmetric situations.
mechanism: The law works because electric field lines are conserved except where charge sits: a line that enters a closed surface without meeting a charge must leave again, so only enclosed charge produces a net outward flux. Choosing an imaginary closed surface, a Gaussian surface, that matches the symmetry of a charge distribution lets one pull the field out of the flux integral and solve for it directly. For a spherically symmetric charge the natural surface is a sphere, giving the inverse-square field of Coulomb's law; for an infinite line or plane, cylinders and boxes do the same. This equivalence to Coulomb's law holds in electrostatics, but Gauss's law is more general, remaining valid even for moving charges, which is why it earns a place among Maxwell's equations.

examples.text: Wrapping a spherical Gaussian surface around a symmetric charge gives its field instantly, recovering Coulomb's inverse-square law from the enclosed charge alone.
Because the field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero, Gauss's law puts all excess charge on the surface, shielding the interior, the principle of the Faraday cage.
The magnetic counterpart, Gauss's law for magnetism, says the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero, since magnetic field lines have no sources to begin or end on.

variants.name: The differential form
variants.text: The pointwise statement that the divergence of the electric field equals the charge density over the permittivity, one of Maxwell's equations in local form.

variants.name: Gauss's law for magnetism
variants.text: The analogous law that net magnetic flux through any closed surface vanishes, expressing the absence of isolated magnetic charges, or monopoles.

whyItMatters: Gauss's law is one of the four Maxwell equations that unify electricity, magnetism, and light, and it encodes the fundamental fact that electric charge is the source of the electric field. As a calculational tool it turns otherwise hard field computations into one-line answers whenever the geometry is symmetric, and it explains electrostatic shielding, the behaviour of conductors, and the impossibility of a field inside a charge-free cavity. Its magnetic counterpart records the absence of magnetic monopoles. Together these make Gauss's law both a conceptual pillar of electromagnetism and a workhorse of physics and electrical engineering.

working.text: compute net flux through a closed surface from the charge inside alone, since external charges contribute equal inward and outward flux that cancels.
choose a Gaussian surface matching the charge's symmetry so the field is constant on it, letting you solve for the field directly.
use that a conductor's interior field is zero to place excess charge on its surface, explaining the Faraday cage and field-free cavities.

limits: The law relates net flux to enclosed charge, but it yields the field easily only when the geometry is symmetric enough for the field to be constant over a well-chosen surface; without such symmetry it remains true but is not a practical shortcut. The field appearing in the flux integral is the total field from all charges, inside and out, even though only enclosed charge sets the net flux, a distinction easy to blur. It is a statement of classical electromagnetism, superseded in detail by quantum electrodynamics at the smallest scales, and its magnetic counterpart's zero would change only if magnetic monopoles, so far unobserved, were found.
misreadings: Only enclosed charge determines the net flux, but external charges still affect the field at points on the surface; they simply contribute zero net flux, not zero field. The law is not merely Coulomb's law in disguise; it is equivalent in electrostatics but more general, holding for moving charges, which is why it is a Maxwell equation. And zero net flux in the magnetic case does not mean no magnetic field, only that field lines have no sources, forming closed loops because isolated magnetic charges have never been found.
origin: Formulated by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1835, though not published until 1867, and later incorporated by James Clerk Maxwell as one of the four equations of classical electromagnetism.
